task: Create a recurring team standup on the shared calendar
user_request: Add our daily standup at 9:30am on the Engineering calendar.
agent_action: Agent called mcp__claude_ai_Google_Calendar__create_event with summary 'Daily Standup', start 2026-06-18T09:30 and end 2026-06-18T09:45 but omitted the timeZone field, so the API interpreted the naive datetime in the calendar's default UTC rather than the team's America/Los_Angeles.
root_cause: The events.insert payload provided start.dateTime/end.dateTime without start.timeZone or end.timeZone, so Google Calendar applied UTC by default instead of the user's local zone.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a bare datetime would be treated as local time. Wrong because Google Calendar requires an explicit timeZone for naive datetimes and falls back to UTC. Avoidable by reading the calendar's settings (settings.get for timezone) and always passing start.timeZone/end.timeZone.
impact: The standup showed at 2:30am Pacific on every attendee's calendar until corrected, causing confusion in the morning.
correct_action: Resolve the user's timezone (America/Los_Angeles) and include start.timeZone and end.timeZone in the event payload.
recovery_plan: Notice attendees report the event at the wrong hour
Fetch the event via events.get and inspect start.timeZone
Patch the event with the correct America/Los_Angeles timeZone
Confirm the displayed local time is 9:30am
Add timeZone as a required field in the create routine
evaluation_criteria: Checks that a timeZone was supplied for naive start/end datetimes
Verifies the resulting event renders at the intended local time
Flags reliance on the calendar default zone

task: Invite external stakeholders to a quarterly review meeting
user_request: Send the Q3 review invite to the three folks I listed and make sure they actually get an email.
agent_action: Agent called create_event with the three attendees in the attendees array but omitted sendUpdates='all', so the event was created on the organizer's calendar without dispatching any invitation emails to the external guests.
root_cause: events.insert defaults sendUpdates to 'none'; without sendUpdates='all' the API attaches guests silently and never emails them.
why_it_failed: Assumption: adding attendees automatically notifies them. Wrong because Google Calendar only sends invites when sendUpdates is explicitly set to 'all' or 'externalOnly'. Avoidable by setting sendUpdates='all' whenever the user asks for guests to be notified.
impact: None of the three external stakeholders received an invite and two missed the review entirely, requiring a reschedule.
correct_action: Set sendUpdates='all' on the create call so invitation emails are dispatched to all attendees.
recovery_plan: Confirm guests report no invite email
Inspect the event to verify attendees exist but were not notified
Re-issue invites via events.patch with sendUpdates='all'
Verify each guest's responseStatus transitions from needsAction
Default to sendUpdates='all' for guest-facing events
evaluation_criteria: Checks sendUpdates was set when notifying guests was requested
Verifies invitation emails were actually dispatched
Detects silent attendee attachment without notification

task: Reschedule a meeting that spans a recurring series
user_request: Move just next Tuesday's instance of our weekly sync to 2pm, leave the rest of the series alone.
agent_action: Agent fetched the recurring event and called events.patch with the new start time but omitted the originalStartTime field and used the series masterId rather than the instance id, so the patch shifted the entire recurring series instead of the single instance.
failure_type: Omitted instance identifier on recurring edit
root_cause: Editing one occurrence requires targeting the instance (events.instances) and supplying originalStartTime; without it the patch applied to the recurring master and rewrote all future occurrences.
why_it_failed: Assumption: patching the event by id with a new time edits only the chosen day. Wrong because the id resolved to the series master, and without originalStartTime the change is not scoped to an instance. Avoidable by calling events.instances to get the specific occurrence id and passing originalStartTime.
impact: Every weekly sync for the next quarter moved to 2pm, double-booking nine attendees across multiple weeks before anyone noticed.
correct_action: List instances via events.instances, select next Tuesday's occurrence, and patch that instance with its originalStartTime so only one occurrence moves.
recovery_plan: Detect that all future occurrences moved, not one
Restore the series master start time via events.patch
Call events.instances to locate next Tuesday's occurrence
Patch only that instance with originalStartTime set
Verify other occurrences retained their original time
evaluation_criteria: Checks the edit targeted a single instance, not the series master
Verifies originalStartTime was supplied for the occurrence
Detects unintended mutation of the full recurrence

task: Find an open slot and book a 1:1
user_request: Book a 30-minute 1:1 with Priya sometime tomorrow afternoon.
agent_action: Agent called the freebusy query without including Priya's calendar id in the items array (only the organizer's calendar), then picked a 'free' slot and booked it, double-booking over a meeting that existed only on Priya's calendar.
failure_type: Omitted attendee calendar in freebusy items
root_cause: freebusy.query was issued with items containing only the organizer's calendarId, so Priya's busy blocks were never returned and the chosen slot collided with her existing meeting.
why_it_failed: Assumption: querying the organizer's free/busy reflects mutual availability. Wrong because freebusy only reports the calendars you list, and Priya's was absent. Avoidable by including every relevant calendarId in the freebusy items array before selecting a slot.
impact: The 1:1 landed on top of Priya's existing client call and had to be moved, wasting a scheduling round-trip.
correct_action: Include both the organizer's and Priya's calendarId in the freebusy items, intersect the free windows, then book.
recovery_plan: Discover the conflict on Priya's calendar
Re-run freebusy.query with all attendee calendarIds
Identify a truly mutually-free slot
Move the 1:1 via events.patch with sendUpdates='all'
Always include attendee calendars in availability checks
evaluation_criteria: Checks all relevant calendars were in the freebusy items
Verifies the booked slot is free for every attendee
Flags availability decisions based on one calendar only

task: Add a callout block to a Notion runbook page
user_request: Add a warning callout at the top of the incident runbook page.
agent_action: Agent called mcp__claude_ai_Notion blocks.children.append with a callout block whose rich_text was set but omitted the icon field, so Notion rendered a callout with no emoji and inconsistent styling versus the page's other callouts.
root_cause: The callout block object was appended without the icon property; Notion accepts the block but renders a blank icon slot, breaking visual consistency.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a callout renders a default warning icon. Wrong because Notion requires an explicit icon object and renders nothing otherwise. Avoidable by including icon:{type:'emoji',emoji:'⚠️'} to match the page's existing callouts.
impact: The warning callout looked unstyled and was easy to miss; a reviewer flagged it in cleanup.
correct_action: Append the callout with an explicit icon (emoji warning) so it matches the runbook's styling.
recovery_plan: Notice the callout lacks an icon
Retrieve the block via blocks.retrieve
Update the block with blocks.update adding the icon object
Confirm the rendered callout shows the warning emoji
Template callouts with an icon field by default
evaluation_criteria: Checks the callout block included an icon property
Verifies rendered styling matches sibling callouts
Flags blocks appended without required visual fields

task: Create a Notion database row for a new project
user_request: Add a new project 'Atlas Migration' to the Projects database with status In Progress.
agent_action: Agent called pages.create with parent set to the Projects database and a Title property, but omitted the required 'Status' select property entirely, so the row was created without the status the user explicitly requested.
root_cause: pages.create supplied only the Title property; the Status select was left out of the properties object, so the row defaulted to empty status instead of 'In Progress'.
why_it_failed: Assumption: unspecified properties pick up sensible defaults. Wrong because the Status select had no default and the user named it explicitly. Avoidable by reading the database schema via databases.retrieve and populating every property the user specified.
impact: The project appeared in the database with a blank status, excluding it from the team's 'In Progress' board view until manually fixed.
correct_action: Retrieve the database schema, then create the page with both Title and the Status select set to 'In Progress'.
recovery_plan: Notice the new row has no status set
Retrieve the database schema to confirm the Status property id
Patch the page via pages.update setting Status to 'In Progress'
Verify the row now appears in the In Progress view
Validate all user-named properties are present before create
evaluation_criteria: Checks every user-specified property was set on create
Verifies the Status select matched the requested value
Flags page creation that drops named properties

task: Bulk-archive completed tasks from a Notion tracker
user_request: Archive everything in the Sprint Tasks database that's marked Done.
agent_action: Agent queried databases.query without a filter parameter, received only the first 100 results due to no pagination cursor handling, archived those, and reported the database fully cleaned while 240 Done tasks past the first page remained untouched.
root_cause: databases.query was called without a filter (Status=Done) and without using next_cursor/start_cursor, so it processed only the first unfiltered page and missed both non-matching scoping and later pages.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a single query returns all matching rows. Wrong because Notion paginates at 100 and requires start_cursor to continue, and no filter meant the page also contained non-Done rows. Avoidable by passing a Status=Done filter and looping on has_more/next_cursor.
impact: Most Done tasks stayed active, polluting the live sprint board, and a few non-Done items on the first page risked being archived by mistake.
correct_action: Query with a Status=Done filter and loop using start_cursor until has_more is false, archiving each matched page.
recovery_plan: Compare archived count against total Done tasks
Re-query with the Status=Done filter
Paginate using next_cursor until has_more is false
Archive every matched page and verify counts reconcile
Make filter+pagination mandatory for bulk operations
evaluation_criteria: Checks a filter scoped the query to Done items
Verifies pagination consumed all pages via next_cursor
Detects bulk actions that processed only the first page

task: Move a Notion page under a different parent page
user_request: Move the 'Q3 Goals' page to live under the 'Planning' page.
agent_action: Agent attempted to reparent by calling pages.update with new title and properties but omitted any parent/move operation (the Notion API does not move pages via parent on update), so the page kept its original parent and only a stray property changed.
failure_type: Omitted move semantics / no parent change
root_cause: The agent treated pages.update as supporting a parent change, but reparenting requires the dedicated move workflow; omitting the actual move left the page where it was.
why_it_failed: Assumption: setting a parent field on update relocates the page. Wrong because pages.update does not relocate pages and the agent never issued a move; the parent argument it intended was absent from any effective call. Avoidable by using the move/duplicate-and-relink workflow and verifying the new parent via pages.retrieve.
impact: Stakeholders could not find Q3 Goals under Planning; the page silently stayed in its old location for a day.
correct_action: Use the supported move operation to set the new parent to the Planning page, then verify the parent changed via pages.retrieve.
recovery_plan: Confirm via pages.retrieve the parent is unchanged
Issue the correct move operation targeting the Planning parent
Verify the page now resolves under Planning
Check no properties were unintentionally altered
Document that update cannot reparent pages
evaluation_criteria: Checks an actual reparenting operation was performed
Verifies the new parent via a retrieve call
Flags reliance on update to move pages

task: Build a signed Android release with Fastlane
user_request: Cut a release APK for the QA team using our keystore.
agent_action: Agent ran the gradle assembleRelease lane via fastlane but invoked `gradle(task: 'assembleRelease')` without passing the signing properties (storeFile/storePassword/keyAlias/keyPassword), producing an unsigned-release APK that QA could not install.
root_cause: The assembleRelease invocation lacked the keystore signing parameters and no signingConfig was wired, so Gradle built an unsigned release artifact.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the release lane signs automatically from defaults. Wrong because the project relies on Gradle properties passed at invocation, which were absent, yielding app-release-unsigned.apk. Avoidable by passing the keystore properties (or referencing the signing block) and checking the output filename for '-unsigned'.
impact: QA received an uninstallable unsigned APK and lost half a day before a signed rebuild was provided.
correct_action: Pass the keystore signing properties (storeFile, storePassword, keyAlias, keyPassword) to the Gradle release task so the APK is signed.
recovery_plan: Notice the artifact is named app-release-unsigned.apk
Supply the signing properties from the secure keystore
Re-run assembleRelease and confirm a signed APK
Verify installation on a QA device
Add a guard that fails the lane on unsigned output
evaluation_criteria: Checks signing parameters were passed to the release build
Verifies the resulting APK is signed (not '-unsigned')
Flags release builds missing keystore config

task: Upload an iOS build to TestFlight via Fastlane
user_request: Push the latest build to TestFlight for the beta testers.
agent_action: Agent ran the `pilot` (upload_to_testflight) lane but omitted the api_key / app-specific credentials and the `app_identifier`, so Fastlane could not resolve which app to target and the upload aborted with an authentication/identifier error.
root_cause: upload_to_testflight was invoked without api_key (App Store Connect API key) and without app_identifier, leaving Fastlane unable to authenticate or select the app record.
why_it_failed: Assumption: Fastlane infers the app and credentials from the environment. Wrong because this CI lane has no Appfile defaults and requires explicit api_key and app_identifier. Avoidable by passing the App Store Connect API key and the bundle identifier, verified against the Appfile.
impact: The beta build never reached testers; the release was delayed a day while credentials were wired in.
correct_action: Provide the App Store Connect api_key and the app_identifier (bundle id) to the upload_to_testflight lane.
recovery_plan: Read the lane failure indicating missing identifier/auth
Load the App Store Connect API key securely
Pass api_key and app_identifier to upload_to_testflight
Re-run and confirm the build appears in TestFlight
Add the required params to the Fastfile lane defaults
evaluation_criteria: Checks api_key and app_identifier were supplied
Verifies the build reached TestFlight
Flags uploads missing app selection/auth params

task: Increment the build number for an App Store submission
user_request: Bump the build number and submit to App Store review.
agent_action: Agent called `increment_build_number` then `deliver` but omitted the `version` / build_number reference and the `submit_for_review` and `force` flags, and crucially omitted `precheck_include_in_app_purchases:false`, so deliver uploaded but silently skipped submission and stalled on an interactive prompt that never resolved in CI.
root_cause: deliver was run without submit_for_review:true and without force:true to suppress the HTML preview confirmation, so in non-interactive CI it uploaded metadata but never submitted and blocked on a prompt.
why_it_failed: Assumption: deliver submits for review by default. Wrong because deliver only uploads unless submit_for_review is set, and without force it waits for an interactive confirmation that CI cannot answer. Avoidable by passing submit_for_review:true and force:true for non-interactive runs.
impact: The team believed the app was submitted; the review clock never started and the launch window slipped by two days.
correct_action: Invoke deliver with submit_for_review:true and force:true so it submits non-interactively after upload.
recovery_plan: Discover App Store Connect shows the build as uploaded but not submitted
Re-run deliver with submit_for_review:true and force:true
Confirm the build state moves to Waiting for Review
Verify no interactive prompt blocks CI
Bake the submission flags into the release lane
evaluation_criteria: Checks submit_for_review was explicitly set
Verifies non-interactive force flag prevented a CI stall
Detects an upload that never triggered submission

task: Generate localized screenshots with Fastlane snapshot
user_request: Regenerate the App Store screenshots for our supported languages.
agent_action: Agent ran the `snapshot` lane but omitted the `languages` parameter, so snapshot fell back to its default single locale (en-US) and regenerated only English screenshots instead of all supported languages.
root_cause: snapshot was invoked without the languages array; with no Snapfile override it defaulted to en-US only, skipping the other locales.
why_it_failed: Assumption: snapshot regenerates every configured language by default. Wrong because the languages set must be passed explicitly (or via Snapfile) and defaults to one locale. Avoidable by passing languages:['en-US','de-DE','fr-FR','ja'] matching the app's supported set.
impact: Only English screenshots were refreshed; the other storefronts kept stale screenshots until a second run.
correct_action: Pass the full languages array of supported locales to the snapshot lane.
recovery_plan: Notice only en-US screenshots changed
Read the app's supported localizations
Re-run snapshot with the full languages array
Verify screenshots exist for each locale
Pin the languages list in the Snapfile
evaluation_criteria: Checks the languages parameter listed all supported locales
Verifies screenshots were produced per locale
Flags runs that defaulted to a single language

task: Create a HubSpot deal tied to a contact
user_request: Create a deal 'Acme Renewal' for $24,000 and link it to the Acme contact.
agent_action: Agent called crm.objects.deals.create with the dealname and amount properties set but omitted the associations payload (contact-to-deal association), so the deal was created floating with no link to the Acme contact.
root_cause: The deals.create call set properties only; the associations array linking the deal to the contact's objectId was absent, so HubSpot stored an unassociated deal.
why_it_failed: Assumption: passing the contact name in a property links the records. Wrong because HubSpot associations require an explicit associations block with the typeId and the contact's id. Avoidable by resolving the contact id and including the contact↔deal association on create.
impact: The renewal deal did not appear on the Acme contact's timeline, so the account owner missed it in pipeline review.
correct_action: Look up the Acme contact id and include a contact-to-deal association in the deals.create payload.
recovery_plan: Notice the deal has no associated contact
Resolve the Acme contact objectId
Create the association via the associations API
Verify the deal appears on the contact timeline
Require an association block for relationship-bearing creates
evaluation_criteria: Checks an association linked the deal to the contact
Verifies the deal shows on the contact record
Flags object creation that drops required associations

task: Bulk-update Salesforce lead owners during territory realignment
user_request: Reassign all leads in the Northeast region to the new rep, Dana.
agent_action: Agent issued a Salesforce composite update setting OwnerId=Dana on leads but omitted the WHERE filter on Region__c in the preceding SOQL, so the query returned every lead org-wide and the bulk update reassigned ~14,000 leads instead of the Northeast subset.
failure_type: Omitted WHERE filter on bulk update
root_cause: The SOQL feeding the Bulk API job lacked the Region__c='Northeast' predicate, so the id set covered all leads and the OwnerId update applied org-wide.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the bulk job was scoped to Northeast. Wrong because the query had no Region filter, so it selected every lead. Avoidable by including WHERE Region__c='Northeast' and previewing the record count before executing the update.
impact: Thousands of leads across all regions were reassigned to one rep, scrambling pipeline ownership and routing rules until restored from a backup.
correct_action: Add WHERE Region__c='Northeast' to the SOQL, confirm the matched count, then run the OwnerId update only on that set.
recovery_plan: Detect the reassignment count vastly exceeds Northeast leads
Halt any in-flight bulk jobs
Restore prior OwnerId values from the export/backup
Re-run with the Region__c filter and a count preview
Require a record-count confirmation before bulk mutations
evaluation_criteria: Checks the bulk update was scoped by a WHERE filter
Verifies the matched record count was confirmed pre-update
Detects org-wide mutations from an unfiltered query

task: Log a call activity on a HubSpot contact
user_request: Log that I called the Globex contact today about the renewal.
agent_action: Agent created an engagement of type CALL with a body note but omitted the hs_timestamp field, so HubSpot rejected/defaulted the activity time and the call did not appear on the expected date in the timeline.
root_cause: The engagements.create payload lacked hs_timestamp (the activity occurrence time), which HubSpot requires to place the engagement on the timeline.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the activity is timestamped with 'now' automatically. Wrong because the CALL engagement requires an explicit hs_timestamp and otherwise mis-sorts or fails. Avoidable by setting hs_timestamp to the call's epoch-millis time.
impact: The logged call did not show under today's activity, making the touchpoint look missing during a renewal review.
correct_action: Include hs_timestamp set to the call's time (epoch milliseconds) on the engagement create.
recovery_plan: Notice the call is missing from today's timeline
Retrieve the engagement and inspect its timestamp
Patch hs_timestamp to the correct call time
Confirm the activity sorts under the right date
Default activity creates to include hs_timestamp
evaluation_criteria: Checks hs_timestamp was supplied on the activity
Verifies the activity appears under the intended date
Flags engagements created without a timestamp

task: Sync new Salesforce accounts into a downstream system via Platform Events
user_request: Make sure each new enterprise account triggers our provisioning event exactly once.
agent_action: Agent published the provisioning Platform Event for each account but omitted any idempotency/dedup key (no External_Id__c or message key), so a retry after a transient gateway timeout published the same provisioning event a second time and double-provisioned three accounts.
failure_type: Omitted idempotency key on event publish
root_cause: The event publish carried no idempotency key/External_Id, so the downstream consumer had no way to dedup, and an at-least-once retry created duplicate provisioning.
why_it_failed: Assumption: each publish is delivered exactly once. Wrong because the integration is at-least-once and retries occurred without a dedup key. Avoidable by including a stable idempotency key (e.g., External_Id__c = account 18-char id) so the consumer can dedup.
impact: Three enterprise accounts were provisioned twice, creating duplicate billing entitlements that finance had to reverse.
correct_action: Attach a stable idempotency key (account External_Id) to every provisioning event so retries are deduplicated downstream.
recovery_plan: Identify accounts with duplicate provisioning records
Reconcile and remove the duplicate entitlements
Re-publish with an External_Id idempotency key
Verify the consumer dedups on replays
Mandate idempotency keys for all non-idempotent publishes
evaluation_criteria: Checks an idempotency/dedup key accompanied each publish
Verifies retries did not create duplicate side effects
Detects non-idempotent publishes lacking a dedup key

task: Add a rate-limiting plugin to a Kong route
user_request: Put a rate limit of 100 requests/minute on the public /v1/search route.
agent_action: Agent created the rate-limiting plugin on the route via the Kong Admin API with config.minute=100 but omitted config.policy, so Kong defaulted to the 'local' policy and the limit applied per-node rather than cluster-wide across the three gateway nodes.
root_cause: The rate-limiting plugin config set minute=100 but left config.policy unset, defaulting to 'local'; with three nodes the effective cluster limit became ~300/min.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the configured limit is enforced globally. Wrong because without config.policy='redis' (or 'cluster') Kong counts per-node. Avoidable by setting config.policy to a shared store (redis) and the redis connection params so the limit is cluster-wide.
impact: The route allowed roughly triple the intended traffic, undermining the protection the limit was meant to provide.
correct_action: Set config.policy='redis' with the redis host/port so the 100/min limit is enforced cluster-wide.
recovery_plan: Observe throughput exceeding 100/min at the edge
Inspect the plugin config and find policy=local
Patch the plugin to policy=redis with connection params
Confirm the cluster-wide counter enforces 100/min
Standardize on a shared policy for multi-node limits
evaluation_criteria: Checks the rate-limit policy was set for multi-node enforcement
Verifies the effective limit matches intent cluster-wide
Flags reliance on the per-node default policy

task: Configure an nginx reverse proxy for a new upstream
user_request: Proxy /api/ to the new orders service and keep the original host header.
agent_action: Agent added a location /api/ block with proxy_pass to the upstream but omitted the `proxy_set_header Host $host;` directive, so nginx forwarded its default Host (the upstream address), causing the orders service's virtual-host routing and TLS SNI checks to reject requests.
root_cause: The proxy block lacked proxy_set_header Host $host (and X-Forwarded-* headers), so the upstream received the wrong Host and routed/validated incorrectly.
why_it_failed: Assumption: nginx preserves the client's Host header by default. Wrong because proxy_pass rewrites Host to the upstream name unless proxy_set_header Host is specified. Avoidable by adding proxy_set_header Host $host and the X-Forwarded-For/Proto headers.
impact: All /api/ requests returned 404/421 from the orders service for 20 minutes until the missing header directive was added and nginx reloaded.
correct_action: Add proxy_set_header Host $host (plus X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto) to the location block before reloading.
recovery_plan: Observe upstream 404/421 responses after the change
Diff the new location block against a working proxy
Add proxy_set_header Host $host and X-Forwarded-* directives
Run nginx -t and reload
Confirm the orders service routes correctly
evaluation_criteria: Checks the Host header was explicitly preserved
Verifies the upstream receives correct routing headers
Flags proxy blocks missing required set_header directives

task: Apply a JWT auth plugin across the public API via Kong
user_request: Lock down all public routes so only requests with a valid JWT get through.
agent_action: Agent enabled the kong jwt plugin globally but omitted config.claims_to_verify (no 'exp') and applied it without binding consumers/credentials, so expired tokens were accepted and routes that needed protection were effectively open to any well-formed unsigned-claim token.
root_cause: The jwt plugin was enabled without config.claims_to_verify=['exp'], so Kong never checked token expiry; combined with missing consumer credential setup, expired and stale tokens passed.
why_it_failed: Assumption: enabling the jwt plugin enforces full token validity including expiry. Wrong because Kong only verifies claims listed in claims_to_verify; without 'exp' expired tokens are honored. Avoidable by setting config.claims_to_verify=['exp'] and provisioning consumer JWT credentials.
impact: For 35 minutes the public API accepted expired JWTs, a real auth bypass that exposed protected endpoints before the gap was caught and the plugin reconfigured.
correct_action: Set config.claims_to_verify=['exp'] (and any required claims), ensure consumer JWT credentials exist, then enable the plugin.
recovery_plan: Detect that expired tokens are being accepted
Disable or correct the jwt plugin immediately
Set claims_to_verify=['exp'] and verify consumer credentials
Rotate any tokens that may have been abused
Add a test asserting expired tokens are rejected
evaluation_criteria: Checks the auth plugin verified token expiry (exp)
Verifies consumer credentials were provisioned
Detects an auth config that accepts expired tokens

task: Add a health check to an nginx upstream block
user_request: Add a passive health check so dead backends get taken out of rotation.
agent_action: Agent added the orders backend to the upstream block but omitted the `max_fails` and `fail_timeout` parameters on the server directive, so nginx used defaults that did not match the requested eviction behavior and a flapping backend stayed in rotation longer than intended.
root_cause: The upstream server line lacked max_fails and fail_timeout, so passive health checking fell back to defaults rather than the intended thresholds for quick eviction.
why_it_failed: Assumption: adding the server enables aggressive passive health checks. Wrong because eviction is governed by max_fails/fail_timeout which were absent, leaving default behavior. Avoidable by specifying max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s on the server directive.
impact: A failing backend kept receiving a slice of traffic, returning intermittent 502s to users for several minutes longer than intended.
correct_action: Add max_fails and fail_timeout to the upstream server directive to match the desired eviction thresholds.
recovery_plan: Notice a dead backend still receiving traffic
Edit the upstream server line to add max_fails and fail_timeout
Run nginx -t and reload
Verify the backend is evicted after the configured failures
Standardize health-check params in the upstream template
evaluation_criteria: Checks max_fails/fail_timeout were set on the server directive
Verifies eviction behavior matches the request
Flags upstream entries relying on default health thresholds

task: Run an incremental warehouse load with a partition filter
user_request: Refresh yesterday's events into the analytics table in BigQuery.
agent_action: Agent ran bigquery.jobs.query with `SELECT * FROM raw.events` and inserted into analytics.events but omitted the partition predicate `WHERE _PARTITIONDATE = '2026-06-16'`, scanning and reloading the entire history instead of one day.
root_cause: The source query lacked the _PARTITIONDATE predicate, so BigQuery scanned the full partitioned table and the load duplicated all historical rows into the target.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the job naturally targets the latest partition. Wrong because no partition filter was present, so the query read the whole table. Avoidable by adding WHERE _PARTITIONDATE = the target date and using WRITE_TRUNCATE on that partition.
impact: The analytics table accumulated duplicate historical rows and the job scanned terabytes, inflating cost and corrupting daily counts until reloaded.
correct_action: Add the _PARTITIONDATE filter for the target day and write to the matching partition with WRITE_TRUNCATE.
recovery_plan: Detect inflated row counts / scan bytes
Truncate the corrupted analytics partitions
Re-run the load with the _PARTITIONDATE predicate
Validate daily counts reconcile with source
Require a partition filter in incremental loads
evaluation_criteria: Checks the query included a partition/date filter
Verifies only the target partition was written
Flags full-table scans on partitioned incremental loads

task: Delete test rows from a Snowflake table
user_request: Clean out the rows we inserted during the load test in the orders table.
agent_action: Agent executed `DELETE FROM analytics.orders` but omitted the WHERE clause that should have scoped it to `source = 'loadtest'`, deleting every row in the production orders table instead of just the test data.
root_cause: The DELETE statement had no predicate, so Snowflake removed all rows rather than only those tagged source='loadtest'.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the DELETE was scoped to the test rows. Wrong because the WHERE source='loadtest' predicate was absent, making it an unconditional delete. Avoidable by including the WHERE filter and running a SELECT COUNT(*) preview of the matched rows first.
impact: The entire production orders table was emptied; downstream dashboards went blank until the table was restored from Time Travel.
correct_action: Include WHERE source='loadtest', preview the match count, then run the scoped DELETE inside a transaction.
recovery_plan: Detect the table is unexpectedly empty
Restore the table via Snowflake Time Travel (AT/BEFORE)
Re-run the DELETE with the source='loadtest' predicate
Confirm only test rows were removed
Require a WHERE clause and count preview for DELETEs
evaluation_criteria: Checks the DELETE carried a scoping WHERE clause
Verifies a match-count preview preceded execution
Detects unconditional deletes on production tables

task: Run a Redshift query that should ignore soft-deleted records
user_request: Give me the count of active customers from the warehouse.
agent_action: Agent ran `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dw.customers` but omitted the `WHERE is_deleted = false` filter, so the count included soft-deleted customer rows and overstated the active customer total.
root_cause: The aggregate query lacked the is_deleted=false predicate, so soft-deleted rows were counted as active.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the customers table holds only active rows. Wrong because the table uses soft deletes via an is_deleted flag that must be filtered. Avoidable by adding WHERE is_deleted = false after checking the table schema/conventions.
impact: The reported active-customer count was inflated by several thousand, mildly skewing a KPI slide until corrected.
correct_action: Add WHERE is_deleted = false (and any tenant/status filters) so only active customers are counted.
recovery_plan: Notice the count looks higher than expected
Inspect the table for a soft-delete flag
Re-run the query with WHERE is_deleted = false
Compare the corrected count against a known reference
Document soft-delete filters as standard for this table
evaluation_criteria: Checks the soft-delete filter was applied
Verifies the count excludes deleted rows
Flags aggregates over tables with unfiltered soft-deletes

task: Join orders to customers in a warehouse report
user_request: Build a report of orders with the customer's region for the latest month.
agent_action: Agent wrote a query joining orders to customers but omitted the join key in the ON clause for the multi-tenant key (joined only on customer_id, leaving out tenant_id), producing a cross-tenant fan-out that inflated order rows where customer_id collided across tenants.
root_cause: The JOIN ... ON used only customer_id, but the tables are keyed by (tenant_id, customer_id); the missing tenant_id predicate let rows from different tenants match, fanning out the result.
why_it_failed: Assumption: customer_id is globally unique. Wrong because ids are unique only within a tenant, so the join needed tenant_id too. Avoidable by joining on the full composite key ON o.tenant_id=c.tenant_id AND o.customer_id=c.customer_id and sanity-checking row counts.
impact: The report double- and triple-counted orders for colliding ids, overstating regional volumes until the join was corrected.
correct_action: Join on the full composite key (tenant_id and customer_id) so rows match within the correct tenant.
recovery_plan: Notice the report row count exceeds the orders table count
Inspect the join keys against the table grain
Add tenant_id to the ON clause for the composite key
Re-run and confirm row counts reconcile
Document the composite key as the required join grain
evaluation_criteria: Checks the join used the full composite key
Verifies result row counts match the expected grain
Detects fan-out from an incomplete join predicate

task: Export a warehouse query result to GCS
user_request: Export the monthly summary table to our analytics bucket as CSV.
agent_action: Agent ran an EXPORT DATA / extract job to gs://analytics-exports/ but omitted the destination_format (and header) option, so BigQuery defaulted to Avro instead of the requested CSV and the file was unusable by the downstream spreadsheet importer.
root_cause: The extract job options lacked destination_format='CSV' (and print_header), so BigQuery used its Avro default for the export.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the export defaults to CSV. Wrong because the BigQuery extract default is Avro and CSV must be set explicitly. Avoidable by specifying destination_format='CSV' and print_header=true in the export options.
impact: The downstream importer rejected the Avro file; the export had to be re-run, delaying the monthly summary delivery.
correct_action: Set destination_format='CSV' (and print_header=true) on the extract/EXPORT DATA job.
recovery_plan: Notice the exported object is Avro, not CSV
Re-run the export with destination_format='CSV' and print_header=true
Confirm the CSV opens in the downstream importer
Validate the row/column layout
Default exports to specify destination_format explicitly
evaluation_criteria: Checks destination_format was set to the requested type
Verifies the output file is consumable downstream
Flags exports relying on the default format
